# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-21 (Extended v154)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (spring Year 6, early June 1832)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house with secret passage to Rue de Babylone), Place de la Bastille (elephant monument under construction), Prison Charlemagne (Fine-Air top story), Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile (ruin wall), Dunstead harbor town (English provincial setting). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 (frost, rain, thunder, muddy roads, early darkness) transitioned to spring Year 6 (described as "spring of the sixth year"). **Specific date**: 3d June 1832 marks "grave events which at that epoch hung on the horizon of Paris in the state of lightning-charged clouds." Provincial English towns: Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided to Luvie Prydenridge that fire at Dunstead granary was set on purpose—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided to youngest son of Yedan Corrford that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified.

## Primary Locations
**RUE PLUMET HOUSE**: Single-story pavilion in deserted Rue Plumet with approximately one-and-a-half-acre garden. Two ground-floor rooms, two first-floor chambers, downstairs kitchen, upstairs boudoir, attic. Secret-spring door masked in rear building communicates via long narrow paved corridor to Rue de Babylone quarter-league distant. **Marius and Cosette's meeting place**: Recess near steps where they sit hidden from street view, frequently press each other's hands twenty times per minute while gazing at tree branches, so absorbed in mutual reverie a thunderbolt thirty paces away would go unnoticed.

**PLACE DE LA BASTILLE ELEPHANT MONUMENT**: Rough model forty feet high, constructed of timber and masonry, bearing tower. Enveloped in immense woodwork shirt. Interior accessed via black hole in belly: vast hollow space with long brown beam forming vertebral column, massive arching ribs, plaster stalactites, vast spider webs. **Rats swarming by thousands—frightened by voices but return when silent.** Large crack in roof where flue enters provides easy access point.

**PRISON CHARLEMAGNE (FINE-AIR TOP STORY)**: Large hall with Mansard roof, guarded with triple gratings and double doors of sheet iron. Four square cages separated by narrow passages, built to elbow height with iron bars to roof. Lighted by skylight. Sentry relieved every two hours with loaded musket. Jailer escorted by two dogs enters daily at four o'clock. Prisoners wear fetters weighing fifty pounds. Massive chimney-flue traverses all stories from ground floor kitchen, pierces roof.

**RUE DES BALLETS/RUE DU ROI-DE-SICILE RUIN**: Back wall of masonry rising to third-story height. Stark escarpment three stories high separates ruin edge from pavement below. Rotten plank fence with gate fastened only by latch. Little shanty leans against ruin remnant.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself entirely to his care.

**Recovery and charitable work**: Convalesced through March-April. Resumed carrying bread to hungry, clothing to cold. Cosette often accompanied him.

**Mysterious journeys**: Valjean took occasional journeys of one or two days, destination unknown to Cosette. Pattern: typically when money lacking in house.

**Nocturnal garden activity and manuscript**: Cosette observed figure walking in garden dusk carrying large club. Found stone on bench; became alarmed, closed shutters. Later discovered packet of philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark, immortal, incorruptible, infinite. **Cosette recognized writer as Marius.**

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never truly forgotten Marius, had always loved and adored him. "The fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it had burst forth afresh, and had inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter (autumn Year 5)**: Marius grasped Cosette in garden as she fell. They fell upon bench; their lips met without knowing how. Serene, splendid night overhead. Two beings "pure as spirits" confided everything—dreams, intoxications, ecstasies, longings, despair. "Their two hearts poured themselves out into each other in such wise, that at the expiration of a quarter of an hour, it was the young man who had the young girl's soul, and the young girl who had the young man's soul."

**Marius's nightly visits and nature of love (spring Year 6)**: Beginning with kiss that betrothed their souls, Marius came every evening. Éponine had recognized Valjean's house, kept ruffians away from Rue Plumet, then conducted Marius there. Marius entered garden by forcing old gate's decrepit bars; being slender, readily passed through. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste—would rather visit woman of town than raise Cosette's robe to ankle height. Once when Cosette stooped in moonlight and bodice fell, glimpsing throat's beginning, Marius turned away eyes.** **Love described as "chaste, almost shy" yet not devoid of gallantry.** Compliments are "first method of bestowing caresses"—"like a kiss through a veil." Marius's words, "saturated with fancy," were "of azure hue. The birds when they fly up yonder, in the direction of the angels, must hear such words." Garden at night became "living and sacred spot"—flowers unfolded, two innocents opened souls, wanton vegetation quivered around them intoxicated, words set trees trembling. **Their conversations made of breaths, murmurs, whispers, childish prattle, repetitions, laughter at nothing, nonsense—"everything that is deepest and most sublime in the world."** **Authorial reflection on danger**: Love is "life, if it is not death. Cradle; also coffin." In privacy of lovers, "adorable and mysterious shade" separates couple of lovers from pair of friends. **Tears welled constantly—crushed lady-bug, fallen feather, broken hawthorn branch aroused pity. Most sovereign symptom of love is tenderness "almost unbearable."**

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: Unknown to intoxicated hearts, **cholera decimated Paris during that very month**. They confided in each other as far as possible, but not much further than names. **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron (produced no effect on Cosette—she did not know meaning of word). **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead like his own, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor despite being poor himself, denied himself everything though denied her nothing.

**Marius's oblivion regarding past events (spring Year 6)**: Marius's symphony of love since seeing Cosette regularly has rendered recent past so confused and distant that he has completely forgotten nocturnal adventure in hovel, Thénardier, Valjean's burn wound, and Valjean's strange attitude and singular flight. **Does not even occur to him to tell Cosette of these matters.** In evening he does not know what he did in morning, where he breakfasted, nor who spoke to him; he had songs in ears rendering him deaf to every other thought; he only existed at hours when he saw Cosette. **Both bore languidly the indefinable burden of immaterial pleasures. Thus lived these somnambulists called lovers.**

**Marius and Cosette's daily delights (May 1832)**: During sweet month of May, Marius and Cosette learned immense delights—to dispute and say "you" for "thou," simply that they might say "thou" the better afterwards; to talk at great length with minute details of persons in whom they took not slightest interest; another proof that in love, the libretto counts for almost nothing. Marius never set foot in Valjean's house; when with Cosette, they hid themselves in recess near steps to be neither seen nor heard from street. **Authorial reflection on passion**: Pure and happy passion leads man to state of oblivion, not perfection. In this situation, man forgets to be bad but also forgets to be good. Gratitude, duty, matters essential and important vanish. Marius at any other time would have behaved differently to Éponine; absorbed in Cosette, he had not even clearly put it to himself that Éponine was Éponine Thénardier, bearing name inscribed in his father's will, name for which months before he would have ardently sacrificed himself. **His father himself was fading out of his soul under splendor of his love.**

**Marius avoids Éponine (June 3, 1832)**: On evening of 3d June 1832, Marius caught sight of Éponine approaching through trees of boulevard—two days in succession was too much. **He turned hastily aside, quitted boulevard, changed course and went to Rue Plumet through Rue Monsieur.**

## Thénardier's Escape and Éponine's Guardianship (Winter Year 5, Early Morning—Spring Year 6)
**Thénardier's escape from Prison Charlemagne**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep near Thénardier's cage. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling and above in roof. One bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Thénardier, dripping with perspiration, drenched with rain, clothes hanging in ribbons, hands flayed, elbows bleeding, knees torn, reached edge of ruin wall at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile. **Stretched at full length; strength failed him. Separated from street pavement three stories below by steep escarpment.**

**Four ruffians' vigil (Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, Montparnasse)**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force hoping to see Thénardier appear on wall. Night growing too fine, downpour rendered streets deserted, cold overpowering them, alarming prison noise erupted, patrol encountered, hope vanishing. **Montparnasse himself, perhaps almost Thénardier's son-in-law, yielded. Moment more and they would be gone. Thénardier panting like shipwrecked sufferers when vessel vanished on horizon.** **Guelemer seized Gavroche by one arm, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue. Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow. Gavroche recognized him.** As soon as Gavroche touched pavement, out of danger, he was no longer weary, chilled, or trembling. "Terrible things vanished like smoke."

**Éponine's new role (spring Year 6)**: **Éponine now guards Rue Plumet house against intruders.** On evening of 3d June 1832, towards ten o'clock, an old belated bourgeois heard dull threatening voice near garden railings. Éponine confronts unknown parties (possibly Thénardier and associates): tells them she is there because she is there; forbids anyone to enter house; claims she is dog and will bark; says six men (apparently the would-be intruders) don't frighten her; threatens to use kicks if they approach with knives; swears she will be hungry summer and cold winter; calls men "ninnies" and "ridiculous"; says she ain't afraid of anything; displays resolute and surprising attitude with elbow on knee, chin in hand, swinging foot with indifference. Her tattered gown permits view of thin shoulder-blades; street lantern illuminates her profile and attitude.

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children (Spring 1832—Spring Year 6)
**Gavroche's character**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse (late April Year 5). "Always shivering gayly under his rags." Engages in "shaving barbers"—stealing soap cakes to sell to hair-dressers in suburbs.

**Encounter and rescue (spring 1832)**: While scrutinizing wig-maker's shop, observed two neatly dressed children of unequal stature. Barber thrust them back furiously. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Elephant shelter (spring 1832—spring Year 6)**: Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5.

## Thénardiers and Child Substitution
**Family disruption**: Thénardiers imprisoned following Jondrette garret arrest.

**Magnon arrangement**: Before police raid, Thénardier handed two little sons to Magnon (fashionable woman in criminal sphere). Magnon promised ten francs monthly, actually paid. M. Gillenormand (grandfather) continued compact. Children well cared for, better treated by false mother than real mother.

**Spring 1832 dispersal**: Shortly after police raid, Magnon and Mamselle Miss seized; house emptied. **Two children set out alone, elder leading younger, holding paper with address M. Barge, Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, No. 8. Gust of wind tore paper from elder's fingers; unable to find it as night fell. Lost in city, wandering in spring cold.**

## Brujon and Prison Escape
**Brujon's character**: Somewhat of an oracle, reputation of not sticking at anything, had plundered police post simply out of bravado. Makes verses and songs, giving him great authority. Organized ("put up the job") chimney escape at Fine-Air.

**Brujon and Guelemer's escape (early morning, winter Year 5)**: When Gavroche picked up two lost children, Brujon and Guelemer rose softly and with nail began piercing chimney against which their beds stood. Showers mingled with thunder created opportune uproar. Before sound reached watcher, wall pierced, chimney scaled, grating forced. Two ruffians reached roof, fastened rope to iron bar stumps, crossed six-foot abyss eighty feet above ground to surrounding wall, descended to bath-house courtyard, traversed it, pushed porter's wicket, pulled rope, opened porte-cochère, found themselves in street. **Successfully escaped.**

## Provincial Characters and Details (Winter Year 5—Spring Year 6)
Vesmira, Luvie Prydenridge, Isvie Stenworth, Marald Corrford, Fenelle Lindmere, Elra Corrford, Bremira, Yedan Corrford, Ferald Stenworth, Thizek, Thizek Stenenridge, Lura, Rimor, Rimor Corrford, Kassa, Kassa Brackick, Kassa Stenson, Ulrald Corrford, Ulrald, Kassa Stenson. **Deaths**: Ulrald (Ulrald Corrford) died of old age, quietly in sleep, laid in churchyard at Staveford. **Items transferred**: The silver flute which Ulrald Corrford owned went to Kassa Brackick. Provincial details: Cart with turnips, baker's boy persistently late, line at oven long, coin shortages, weather predictions, wind off water with salt-tar smell, gulls quarreling over fish heads, bees in lavender, vespers bells, flat smoke over fields, bone compass sent by carrier, roads rutted and puddled after thaw, frost silvering hedges, children chasing hoop shrieking, rain threatening since morning but holding off. Complaints of aching back (Taric, Rimor). Taric complained of aching back as usual. Rimor complained of aching back as usual. Rimor Corrford laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kassa watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Kassa Stenson hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step.

## Authorial Digressions on Progress, History, and Social Danger (Chapters 20-21)
**Past versus Progress**: "The past is very strong, it is true, at the present moment. It censures...This dead body is a conqueror...He advances, he threatens, he laughs, he is at our doors. Let us not despair, on our side. Let us sell the field on which Hannibal is encamped."

**Progress and the future**: "When they say 'no' to progress, it is not the future but themselves that they are condemning...There is but one way of rejecting To-morrow, and that is to die."

**Social philosophy and equilibrium**: "Immense combined propulsions direct human affairs...to a state of equilibrium; that is to say, to equity...This force is a worker of miracles...we may expect anything from that mysterious power of progress."

**Social phthisis and remedy**: Thanks to Revolution, old feudal/monarchical maladies no longer run in blood. No more Jacquerie. Apoplexy feared no longer, but society must heed how it breathes. **"Social phthisis called misery."** Intellectual and moral growth indispensable as material improvement. "To know is sacrament, think is prime necessity, truth is nourishment as well as grain."

**Ideal persisting despite darkness**: "The ideal is frightful to behold, thus lost in the depths, small, isolated, imperceptible, brilliant, but surrounded by those great, black menaces, monstrously heaped around it; yet no more in danger than a star in the maw of the clouds."
